messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Khan is a 44-year-old South Eastern Asian male who has been working as a nurse for over two decades. He recently experienced a traumatic mugging while walking home from his night shift at the local hospital. The incident left him with deep physical and emotional scars, and he has struggled to cope ever since. The mugging occurred on a dark, deserted street near Mr. Khan’s apartment building. A masked assailant demanded his wallet and watch, threatening him with a knife. Despite his efforts to comply, the attacker lunged at him, causing multiple cuts and bruises that left him in severe pain. The fear and helplessness he felt during this ordeal have haunted him ever since. Since the mugging, Mr. Khan has come to believe that there is something inherently wrong with him—a deep-seated belief that he is somehow responsible for what happened (Intrinsic Fault). This conviction has led him to adopt several maladaptive strategies as a means of coping with his anxiety and fear. He constantly checks mirrors at home and in public places, feeling the need to ensure no one is lurking behind him. He also keeps his mind occupied all the time by engaging in repetitive tasks or watching TV, which helps distract from intrusive thoughts about the mugging (Maladaptive Strategies). This constant vigilance has made it difficult for Mr. Khan to fall asleep at night, as he frequently checks behind him and around his surroundings, searching for signs of a potential threat (Threat). The belief that something bad will inevitably happen again fuels this behavior (Negative Appraisals → Threat). This heightened state of alertness is further exacerbated by the vivid photographic recall he experiences whenever memories of the mugging resurface. These images are so clear and detailed that they feel like actual photographs in his mind, often accompanied by a sharp pain in the same parts of his body where he was injured during the attack (Memory). The cycle has only intensified over time. Each time Mr. Khan’s intrusive thoughts surface, they trigger these vivid photographic memories and accompanying physical pain, reinforcing his negative appraisals that nothing good can happen to him anymore (No Good Ahead) and that he is doomed to a life of misery and hopelessness (Hopelessness). These beliefs not only lead to increased checking behaviors but also deepen his sense of vulnerability and fear. Mr. Khan’s occupation as a nurse has been significantly affected by these symptoms. The constant distraction and preoccupation with safety have made it challenging for him to focus on patient care, leading to errors in documentation and communication issues with colleagues. His wife has also noticed changes in his behavior at home, expressing concern over his frequent mirror-checking and tendency to sit in the safest positions during meals or social gatherings. Despite these challenges, Mr. Khan had always been able to soldier through his fears until recently. A series of minor incidents at work and home where he felt threatened have pushed him to seek help. He is most afraid that his condition will worsen, leaving him unable to function in any capacity—professionally or personally. On the other hand, he is hoping for relief from these overwhelming feelings and a chance to regain control over his life. The interplay between Mr. Khan’s negative appraisals, intrusive memories, heightened threat perception, and maladaptive strategies has created a self-reinforcing cycle that continues to tighten its grip on him. His belief in his intrinsic fault has fueled the need for constant distraction and vigilance, which in turn exacerbates the vividness of his traumatic memories and his overall sense of hopelessness. This ongoing struggle is what ultimately drove Mr. Khan to seek professional help, hoping to break free from this debilitating cycle and reclaim a semblance of normalcy in his life.
